blocks.text: Almost everyone in Turkey knows a dozen stories about Nasreddin Hoca: a small man with a big turban, a grey donkey and an answer for everything. A *hoca* is a teacher, and in his day also a man of religious learning. His stories are told from the Balkans to China, and he goes by other names along the way: Molla Nasreddin in Azerbaijan, Afandi or Apendi in Central Asia.

Tradition places him in 13th-century Anatolia. The account most often repeated, which goes back to a 19th-century mufti of Sivrihisar, says he was born in 1208 in the village of Hortu, near Sivrihisar, served as its imam, settled in Akşehir in 1237, worked there as a teacher and judge, and died there in 1284. Historians treat these dates with caution. The oldest text that mentions him, the *Saltukname*, was written around 1480, and the earliest dated collection of his anecdotes, with 43 stories, comes from 1571.

His tomb in Akşehir has a large padlock on its door, and every July the town holds a festival in his honour. About 300 anecdotes are attributed to him today, some borrowed over the centuries from other storytellers. They are short, and they end on a twist: a reply that sounds foolish and turns out to be wise.

In one, the Hoca goes to a banquet in his everyday clothes and nobody offers him a seat. He goes home, puts on a fine fur coat and comes back, and now he is led to the best place at the table. When the soup arrives, he dips his sleeve in it: *Ye kürküm ye!* (Eat, my coat, eat!). Since it was the coat they welcomed, the coat should have the soup. The phrase is still used for people who are judged by their clothes.

In another, he borrows a neighbour's cauldron and returns it with a little pot inside: the cauldron, he says, has given birth. The neighbour happily keeps both. Next time, the Hoca keeps the cauldron and announces that it has died. A cauldron can't die, protests the neighbour. You believed it could give birth, the Hoca replies.

The best known of all shows the Hoca as a judge (*kadı*). The first man tells his side of a quarrel, and the Hoca says: you're right. The second man tells the opposite story, and the Hoca says: you're right. His wife, who has been listening, protests that they can't both be right. The Hoca thinks for a moment and says: you're right too.

In 2022 UNESCO added the tradition of telling Nasreddin anecdotes to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, at the joint request of seven countries: Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

blocks.title: The grammar of the punchline
blocks.text: The last line of the judge story is pure unit 4: *Sen de haklısın*, you're right **too**, with *de* written apart. Older Turkish speakers sometimes call their wife *hanım*, and that is how the Hoca addresses her below.
Here is the judge story in the Turkish you know:

lines.tr: Ahmet haklı, Mehmet de haklı, öyle mi?
lines.en: Ahmet is right, and Mehmet is right too, is that it?

questions.q: In which town is Nasreddin Hoca's tomb?
questions.explain: Tradition says he settled in Akşehir in 1237 and died there; the town holds a festival for him every July.

questions.q: What does the Hoca say to his wife at the end of the judge story?
questions.explain: *Sen de haklısın*: *de* adds her to the people who are right.
